newsitem.title: FRANCE: French-Italy ATR awaits Florence accident details.
newsitem.headline: French-Italy ATR awaits Florence accident details.

text.p: A spokesman for Franco-Italian plane-maker ATR said on Wednesday it did not know the cause of a runway overshoot at Florence airport which left a pilot in hospital in a coma.
"We have no information on the cause," a company spokesman told Reuters from ATR headquarters in Toulouse, southwest France. "We are waiting for information from the airline."

An ATR-42 turboprop plane operated by French private airline Air Littoral failed to stop at the end of the runway after landing at the small Florence airport, broke through the perimeter fence and hit a motorway guard rail.
The spokesman said one pilot had suffered head injuries and the other had both legs broken.
None of the 14 passengers was seriously injured.
The two "black box" recorders which record flight and instrument data have been recovered. The spokesman said the read out should take about a week.

The Air Littoral plane was the latest model in the ATR 42 family built by Avions de Transport Regional, a joint venture between France's state-owned Aerospatiale and Alenia, a unit of the Italian Finmeccanica group.

ATR ploughed $100 million into upgrading the ATR 42 with the 500 and 210A models, which have a redesigned cabin interior and lower noise and vibration levels normally associated with turboprop planes. The aircraft are powered by two Pratt & Whitney engines, each sporting distinctive six-bladed Hamilton Standard propellers.
Pratt & Whitney and Hamilton Standard are subsidiaries of the U.S. United Technologies Corp group.
The ATR 42-500 seats up to 46 passengers and can take off and land in 700 metres. The Florence runway measures 1,600 metres, the spokesman said.
ATR has sold 551 of its planes since the early 1980s. The ATR aircraft is marketed by the Aero International (Regional) consortium which groups Aerospatiale, Alenia and British Aerospace Plc.

The plane in the Florence incident entered service in March 1996 and had accumulated around 2,300 flight hours, the spokesman said. It would have typically flown the Nice-Florence route around a couple of times a day.

Montpellier-based Air Littoral specialises in short hops in the southern Mediterranean region and has a fleet of 15 ATR 42 500s. The airline recently agreed a joint marketing pact with Germany's Lufthansa.
